title: Carbohydrate Chemistry — Lecture I
summary: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or substances that yield these on hydrolysis; they contain C, H, and O with H:O in a 2:1 ratio, giving the general formula (CH2O)n and the name 'hydrates of carbon'.

Biologically, carbohydrates provide energy through oxidation, supply carbon for cell components (e.g., ribose in nucleic acids), serve as stored chemical energy, and form part of cell and tissue structures.

Carbohydrates are classified into monosaccharides (simplest), disaccharides (2 monosaccharides on hydrolysis), oligosaccharides (3–10 monosaccharides), and polysaccharides (more than 10 monosaccharides).
Monosaccharides are classified by carbon number (triose, tetrose, pentose, hexose) and by functional group as aldoses (aldehyde prefix aldo-) or ketoses (ketone prefix keto-).
Chirality arises when a carbon is attached to four different groups; a molecule with n chiral carbons has at most 2^n possible stereoisomers.
Fischer projections place the carbonyl group at the top and the last CH2OH at the bottom; D/L designation is determined by the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group.
Optical activity: levorotatory (−) rotates polarized light left, dextrorotatory (+) rotates it right; a racemic mixture is optically inactive because the two enantiomers cancel each other.
Epimers are stereoisomers that differ at only one asymmetric carbon; monosaccharides exist in solution mainly as cyclic hemiacetals/hemiketals with α and β anomers at the anomeric carbon.
Chemical reactions include oxidation (gluconic, glucuronic, glucaric acids), phosphate ester formation at C6, and glycoside formation; reducing sugars react with Benedict's reagent.
Polysaccharides include starch (amylose and amylopectin), glycogen (highly branched), cellulose (β-linkages, structural), and heteropolysaccharides (hyaluronic acid, heparin, chondroitin).

keyTerms.definition: A polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone, or a substance that yields such compounds on hydrolysis; contains C, H, and O with the general formula (CH2O)n.
The simplest carbohydrate, containing only one polyhydroxy aldehyde or ketone unit; classified by carbon number and functional group.
A carbon atom attached to four different groups; it produces two non-superimposable mirror images and is a center of chirality.
Two stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other, such as D- and L-glyceraldehyde.
A 2D representation of a molecule placing the carbonyl group at or near the top and the last achiral CH2OH at the bottom; horizontal bonds point toward the viewer, vertical bonds away.
Stereoisomers that differ in the configuration of the OH group at only one asymmetric carbon.
The carbon that carries the aldehyde or ketone group and is involved in cyclization; it becomes a new chiral center generating α and β anomers.
A sugar with a free hemiacetal that reduces Cu2+ in Benedict's reagent to a red-orange precipitate of Cu2O; all monosaccharides are reducing sugars.
The new carbon-oxygen bond formed between the anomeric carbon of a sugar and an alcohol (or another sugar), producing a glycoside.
A long unbranched chain of repeating disaccharide units composed of amino sugars and uronic acids; when bound to protein it forms glycoproteins.
A monosaccharide in which a hydroxyl group (usually at C2) has been replaced by an amino group; examples include D-glucosamine and D-galactosamine.
A monosaccharide in which the terminal CH2OH has been oxidized to a carboxylic acid (e.g., D-glucuronic acid).
The change in optical rotation when α- and β-anomers of a sugar interconvert in solution via the open-chain form.
A compound closely associated with living organisms; includes carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.

flashcards.front: What is the general formula of carbohydrates and why are they called 'hydrates of carbon'?
flashcards.back: (CH2O)n; the name comes from the observation that heating sugars yields carbon and water, with H and O in a 2:1 ratio.

flashcards.front: How are carbohydrates classified on hydrolysis?
flashcards.back: Monosaccharides (simplest, one unit), disaccharides (2 units), oligosaccharides (3–10 units), and polysaccharides (more than 10 units).

flashcards.front: What is the maximum number of stereoisomers for a molecule with n chiral carbons?
How do you assign D or L configuration in a Fischer projection of a carbohydrate?
flashcards.back: Look at the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group: OH on the right = D-isomer; OH on the left = L-isomer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between enantiomers and epimers?
flashcards.back: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images differing at all chiral centers; epimers differ at only one chiral center.

flashcards.front: Why is sucrose a non-reducing sugar?
flashcards.back: Both anomeric carbons of glucose and fructose are involved in the glycosidic linkage, so neither ring can open to the free aldehyde/ketone.

flashcards.front: What color does amylose give with iodine and why?
flashcards.back: A deep blue-purple color, because amylose helices trap iodine molecules inside the helical chain.

flashcards.front: What monosaccharide units make up heparin, and what is its biological role?
flashcards.back: Sulfated glucuronic acid and sulfated glucosamine joined by α-1,4 bonds; heparin acts as an anticoagulant.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a homo-polysaccharide and a heteropolysaccharide?
flashcards.back: Homo-polysaccharides yield only one type of monosaccharide on hydrolysis (e.g., starch, glycogen, cellulose); heteropolysaccharides contain a mixture of monosaccharides and include amino sugars and uronic acids.

flashcards.front: Which polysaccharide is the single most abundant organic compound on Earth?
flashcards.back: Cellulose, the structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls; wood is about 50% cellulose.

flashcards.front: How do ruminants (cows, sheep, goats) digest cellulose?
flashcards.back: They rely on colonies of symbiotic bacteria in the digestive system that produce enzymes capable of breaking down cellulose, plus a series of stomachs to give cellulose more time to digest.

flashcards.front: What is an amino sugar, and give two examples.
flashcards.back: An amino sugar has an OH replaced by an NH2 group (usually at C2); examples are D-glucosamine and D-galactosamine.
The interconversion of α- and β-anomers through the open-chain form in solution, producing a change in optical rotation until equilibrium is reached.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a glycoprotein and a mucopolysaccharide?
flashcards.back: Glycoproteins are proteins covalently linked to carbohydrate chains; mucopolysaccharides (heteropolysaccharides) are long carbohydrate chains that, when bound to protein, form glycoproteins.

questions.question: Which of the following statements best defines carbohydrates according to the lecture?
options: They are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or substances that yield such compounds on hydrolysis
They are polyhydroxy alcohols that never contain a carbonyl group
They are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds
They are nonpolar lipids composed entirely of carbon and hydrogen
questions.explanation: The lecture defines carbohydrates (saccharides) as polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or substances that yield such compounds on hydrolysis.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the definition in the lecture.
Incorrect. Polyhydroxy alcohols lack the carbonyl group that defines carbohydrates.
Incorrect. Amino acid polymers are proteins.
Incorrect. Lipids are not carbohydrates and are not defined by carbonyl groups.
questions.hint: Focus on the carbonyl (aldehyde/ketone) functional group.

questions.question: Why are carbohydrates referred to as 'hydrates of carbon'?
options: Because they contain only hydrogen and water
Because heating sugars yields carbon and water, and H:O is roughly 2:1
Because they are always crystalline solids that dissolve in water
Because they contain nitrogen and sulfur in addition to carbon
questions.explanation: The name comes from heating sugars, which produces carbon and water; the H:O ratio is 2:1, giving the general formula (CH2O)n.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
Correct. Carbon and water are products of heating, matching the 2:1 H:O ratio.
Incorrect. Solubility in water does not explain the name.
Incorrect. Carbohydrates do not characteristically contain nitrogen or sulfur.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when sugar is heated.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a biological role of carbohydrates listed in the lecture?
options: Supplying carbon for synthesis of cell components such as ribose in nucleic acids
Acting as the primary catalyst of enzyme reactions
questions.explanation: The lecture lists energy supply, carbon supply, storage of chemical energy, and structural roles. Carbohydrates are not described as the primary catalysts of enzyme reactions.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Energy through oxidation is listed.
Incorrect. Supplying carbon for ribose synthesis is listed.
Incorrect. Stored chemical energy is listed.
Correct. Enzymes are typically proteins, not carbohydrates.
questions.hint: Which option sounds like a protein function?

questions.question: According to the classification scheme in the lecture, an oligosaccharide yields on hydrolysis:
questions.explanation: Oligosaccharides on hydrolysis give 3 to 10 monosaccharides.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That describes a disaccharide.
Correct. This is the lecture's definition of oligosaccharides.
Incorrect. That describes a polysaccharide.
Incorrect. That describes a monosaccharide.
questions.hint: Look at the range quoted for oligosaccharides.

questions.question: A polysaccharide is defined in the lecture as a carbohydrate that on hydrolysis gives:
questions.explanation: Polysaccharides on hydrolysis give more than 10 monosaccharide units.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That describes a disaccharide.
Incorrect. That describes an oligosaccharide.
Correct. Polysaccharides yield more than 10 monosaccharides.
Incorrect. Amino sugars are a component of some heteropolysaccharides, not the definition of a polysaccharide.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a monosaccharide class with its carbon count?
questions.explanation: Pentoses contain 5 carbon atoms, as listed in the classification table.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Trioses contain 3 carbons.
Incorrect. Tetroses contain 4 carbons.
Correct. Pentoses contain 5 carbons.
Incorrect. Hexoses contain 6 carbons.
questions.hint: Match the prefix to the number: tri-, tetr-, pent-, hex-.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct ketose example for a hexose?
questions.explanation: Fructose is the ketose example for hexoses in the lecture's classification.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose is an aldose hexose.
Correct. Fructose is the ketose hexose example.
Incorrect. Ribose is an aldose pentose.
Incorrect. Erythrose is an aldose tetrose.
questions.hint: Look at the C6H12O6 ketose row.

questions.question: The prefixes aldo- and keto- in monosaccharide names indicate:
options: The number of carbons in the chain
The presence of an aldehyde or a ketone group respectively
The stereochemistry at the anomeric carbon
The type of glycosidic linkage present
questions.explanation: Aldo- indicates an aldehyde group, and keto- indicates a ketone group, per the lecture's classification rule.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Carbon number is described by tri-, tetr-, pent-, hex-.
Correct. Aldo- = aldehyde; keto- = ketone.
Incorrect. Anomeric configuration is described by α- and β-.
Incorrect. Glycosidic linkages are described by α/β and the carbon numbers involved.
questions.hint: Match each prefix to the functional group.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about chirality is correct according to the lecture?
options: A carbon attached to four identical groups is chiral
A carbon attached to four different groups is chiral and has two non-superimposable mirror images
All carbons in organic compounds are chiral
Chirality requires at least two asymmetric carbons
questions.explanation: A chiral carbon is bonded to four different groups and exists as two non-superimposable mirror images.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Four identical groups would make the carbon achiral.
Correct. This is the definition of a chiral carbon.
Incorrect. Many carbons (e.g., CH3) are achiral.
Incorrect. A single chiral carbon is enough for chirality (e.g., glyceraldehyde).
questions.hint: All four substituents must be different.

questions.question: Which of the following objects is described in the lecture as achiral?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists drinking glasses, spheres, and cubes as achiral objects that can be superimposed on their mirror images.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Hands are chiral.
Incorrect. Gloves are chiral.
Correct. Drinking glasses are listed as achiral.
Incorrect. Shoes are chiral.
questions.hint: Achiral = superimposable on its mirror image.

questions.question: If a molecule has 4 chiral carbons, what is the maximum number of possible stereoisomers according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The formula is 2^n; with n = 4, that gives 2^4 = 16 stereoisomers.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This equals n, not 2^n.
Incorrect. 2^3 = 8 corresponds to 3 chiral carbons.
Correct. 2^4 = 16.
Incorrect. 2^5 = 32 corresponds to 5 chiral carbons.

questions.question: Cholesterol has 8 chiral carbons. How many stereoisomers are theoretically possible, and how many does nature make?
questions.explanation: The lecture computes 2^8 = 256 possible stereoisomers, but nature makes only one.
optionExplanations: Correct. 2^8 = 256; only one occurs in nature.
Incorrect. 2^7 = 128 corresponds to 7 chiral carbons.
Incorrect. 2^6 = 64 corresponds to 6 chiral carbons.
Incorrect. 2^9 = 512 corresponds to 9 chiral carbons.
questions.hint: Watch both halves of the answer.

questions.question: In a Fischer projection of a carbohydrate, the D- or L- designation is determined by the orientation of the OH group on:
options: The chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group
The chiral carbon nearest the carbonyl group
questions.explanation: The lecture specifies that for carbohydrates with more than one chiral center, the D/L designation looks at the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The anomeric carbon determines α/β, not D/L.
Correct. This is the standard rule stated in the lecture.
Incorrect. The nearest chiral carbon does not determine D/L.
Incorrect. The terminal CH2OH is achiral.

questions.question: In carbohydrate chemistry, the D/L designation of a monosaccharide refers to the configuration at the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group and is independent of which property?
questions.explanation: The D/L nomenclature reflects the spatial configuration of the reference carbon and does NOT indicate the direction in which the molecule rotates plane-polarized light; that is described by (+) and (−).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Melting point is a physical property unrelated to D/L notation.
Correct. D/L is independent of optical rotation direction.
Incorrect. Solubility does not define D or L.
Incorrect. Molecular weight is identical for both enantiomers.
questions.hint: D does not automatically mean dextrorotatory.

questions.question: Which compound is described as the simplest carbohydrate, existing in two isomeric mirror-image forms?
questions.explanation: Glyceraldehyde is described as the simplest carbohydrate and exists as two mirror-image isomers (D and L).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose is a hexose with four chiral centers.
Correct. Glyceraldehyde is the simplest carbohydrate.
Incorrect. Fructose is a ketohexose.
Incorrect. Erythrose is a tetrose.
questions.hint: The simplest carbohydrate is a triose.

questions.question: Why are most animals, including humans, unable to digest cellulose?
options: Cellulose is not a polymer of glucose
Cellulose contains β(1→4) linkages that most animals lack the enzymes to break
Cellulose contains no glycosidic bonds at all
Cellulose is too large to enter the digestive system
questions.explanation: Most animals lack the enzyme capable of breaking the β(1→4) glycosidic linkages in cellulose; ruminants rely on symbiotic bacteria instead.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Cellulose is a polymer of D-glucose.
Correct. The β(1→4) linkages resist normal digestive enzymes.
Incorrect. Cellulose contains β(1→4) glycosidic bonds.
Incorrect. Size is not the reason for indigestibility.
questions.hint: What type of linkage does cellulose use?

questions.question: Which of the following pairs are enantiomers of each other?
questions.explanation: By definition, the D- and L- forms of the same monosaccharide are enantiomers (non-superimposable mirror images).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose and fructose are structural isomers with different functional groups.
Incorrect. Maltose and sucrose are different disaccharides.
Correct. D and L forms of the same sugar are enantiomers.
Incorrect. Amylose and cellulose are different glucose polymers with different linkages.
questions.hint: Enantiomers are mirror images of the same molecule.

questions.question: Which of the following best defines epimers?
options: Stereoisomers that are mirror images of each other at every chiral center
Stereoisomers that differ in the position of the OH group at only one asymmetric carbon
Structural isomers with different functional groups
Compounds that rotate polarized light in opposite directions but are not mirror images
questions.explanation: Epimers are stereoisomers that differ at only one asymmetric carbon.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Differing at every chiral center describes enantiomers.
Correct. This is the lecture's definition of epimers.
Incorrect. Structural isomers differ in connectivity, not stereochemistry.
Incorrect. This describes enantiomers with opposite optical rotation.

questions.question: A dextrorotatory substance is one that:
options: Rotates polarized light to the left
Rotates polarized light to the right
questions.explanation: A dextrorotatory (+) substance rotates polarized light to the right; a levorotatory (−) substance rotates it to the left.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Rotating to the left is levorotatory.
Correct. Dextrorotatory = rotates to the right.
Incorrect. Optically inactive substances do not rotate light; dextrorotatory substances do.
Incorrect. Dextrorotatory substances are optically active.

questions.question: A racemic mixture is optically inactive because:
options: It contains equal quantities of two enantiomers whose rotatory effects cancel each other
questions.explanation: A racemate contains equal amounts of the (+) and (−) enantiomers; their rotatory effects cancel, making the mixture optically inactive.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. One enantiomer alone would be optically active.
Correct. Equal and opposite rotations cancel out.
Incorrect. Racemic mixtures contain chiral molecules.
Incorrect. Racemates are made of chiral molecules.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between enantiomers and optical rotation?
options: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light in the same direction
Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions by the same magnitude
Enantiomers do not contain chiral carbons
questions.explanation: Enantiomers have identical physical properties except that they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions by the same magnitude.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They rotate in opposite directions.
Correct. Opposite rotations of equal magnitude.
Incorrect. Enantiomers are optically active.
Incorrect. Enantiomers are chiral by definition.
questions.hint: Only the direction, not the amount, differs.

questions.question: Which biological fact is stated in the lecture about L- and D-lactic acid?
options: L-lactic acid is found in living muscles; D-lactic acid is present in sour milk
L-lactic acid is present in sour milk; D-lactic acid is found in living muscles
Both forms are equally abundant in human muscle
questions.explanation: The lecture states that L-lactic acid is found in living muscles while D-lactic acid is present in sour milk.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the lecture statement.
Incorrect. The two assignments are reversed.
Incorrect. The two forms occur in different biological contexts.
Incorrect. Both forms are optically active.

questions.question: Which drug is mentioned in the lecture as an example where one enantiomer is beneficial and the other is a poison?
questions.explanation: The lecture cites thalidomide as a case where one enantiomer is beneficial while the enantiomer is a poison.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Penicillin is not used as the enantiomer example.
Correct. Thalidomide is the classic example cited.
Incorrect. Aspirin is not discussed for chirality in this lecture.
Incorrect. Ibuprofen is not mentioned in this lecture.
questions.hint: It is a famous historical chiral drug.

questions.question: According to the lecture, which statement about human metabolism of monosaccharides is correct?
options: Humans can metabolize both D- and L-monosaccharides equally
Humans can metabolize D-monosaccharides but not L-isomers
Human metabolism does not depend on stereochemistry
questions.explanation: The lecture states that humans can metabolize D-monosaccharides but not L-isomers; only L-amino acids are used in protein synthesis.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Humans cannot metabolize L-monosaccharides.
Correct. This matches the lecture.
Incorrect. The reverse is stated: only D-monosaccharides are metabolized.
Incorrect. The lecture emphasizes stereochemical specificity.
questions.hint: Which isomer is used for energy?

questions.question: Which of the following physical properties of monosaccharides is stated in the lecture?
options: They are gases at room temperature
They are sweet-tasting solids, with fructose being the sweetest
questions.explanation: The lecture states monosaccharides are sweet-tasting solids at room temperature, with fructose being the sweetest (73% sweeter than sucrose).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They are solids at room temperature.
Correct. They are sweet solids; fructose is the sweetest.
Incorrect. They are extremely water soluble due to their many OH groups.
Incorrect. The lecture does not state they are colored.

questions.question: Which monosaccharide is described in the lecture as the sweetest, being about 73% sweeter than sucrose?
questions.explanation: Fructose is the sweetest monosaccharide — about 73% sweeter than sucrose, which is why less fructose is needed to sweeten foods.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose is less sweet than fructose.
Correct. Fructose is the sweetest monosaccharide.
Incorrect. Galactose is less sweet than fructose.
Incorrect. Ribose is not noted for its sweetness.
questions.hint: It is present in honey and fruits.

questions.question: Why are monosaccharides so soluble in water despite their relatively high molecular weights?
options: Because they contain many hydroxyl (OH) groups capable of hydrogen bonding with water
Because they contain long hydrocarbon chains
questions.explanation: The presence of large numbers of OH groups makes monosaccharides much more water soluble than most molecules of similar molecular weight.
optionExplanations: Correct. OH groups hydrogen bond with water.
Incorrect. Monosaccharides are generally nonionic in their cyclic form.
Incorrect. Long hydrocarbon chains would decrease solubility.
Incorrect. Monosaccharides do not contain heavy metals.

questions.question: The approximate solubility of glucose in water, as stated in the lecture, is:
options: 1 g per 1 mL of water, forming a syrup
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that glucose can dissolve in minute amounts of water to make a syrup (1 g / 1 mL H2O).
optionExplanations: Correct. 1 g / 1 mL H2O forming a syrup.
Incorrect. That would be very dilute.
Incorrect. That would be extremely dilute.
Incorrect. Glucose is highly soluble.
questions.hint: It forms a syrup at this concentration.

questions.question: Monosaccharides in solution usually exist primarily as:
options: Cyclic hemiacetal or hemiketal ring structures
questions.explanation: Monosaccharides do not usually exist in solution in their open-chain forms; an alcohol group adds to the carbonyl to form a stable cyclic hemiacetal or hemiketal.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Open-chain forms are a very small fraction in solution.
Correct. Cyclic hemiacetal/hemiketal forms dominate.
Incorrect. Monosaccharides are not free radicals.
Incorrect. They are not hydrocarbons.

questions.question: The six-membered cyclic form of a monosaccharide is called a pyranose. The five-membered cyclic form is called:
questions.explanation: The five-membered ring is a furanose; the six-membered ring is a pyranose.
optionExplanations: Correct. Five-membered rings are furanoses.
Incorrect. Pyranose is the six-membered ring.
Incorrect. Anomer refers to α/β configuration at C1.
Incorrect. Epimer refers to differences at one chiral carbon.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the anomeric carbon is correct?
options: It is only present in ketoses
It is the carbon that carries the carbonyl group and becomes a new chiral center on cyclization
It is always the terminal CH2OH carbon
It is never involved in glycosidic bond formation
questions.explanation: The anomeric carbon carries the aldehyde or ketone group and, on cyclization, becomes a new chiral center generating α and β anomers.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Anomeric carbons exist in both aldoses and ketoses.
Correct. This is the definition of the anomeric carbon.
Incorrect. The terminal CH2OH is not the anomeric carbon.
Incorrect. It is the site of glycosidic bond formation.
questions.hint: It is the carbonyl carbon of the open-chain form.

questions.question: In the α-anomer of D-glucose, the OH group on the anomeric carbon points:
questions.explanation: In α-D-glucose the OH group on C1 points down; in β-D-glucose it points up.
optionExplanations: Correct. α = OH down.
Incorrect. OH up corresponds to β.
Incorrect. Left/right is not the α/β designation.
Incorrect. Left/right is not the α/β designation.
questions.hint: α = down (in the standard Haworth drawing for D-glucose).

questions.question: In the pyranose form of glucose, β-D-glucose is the anomer in which the OH on C1 points:
questions.explanation: The β-anomer has the OH group on the anomeric carbon pointing up in the standard Haworth representation for D-glucose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. OH down is α.
Correct. β = OH up.
Incorrect. Left/right is not α/β.
Incorrect. Left/right is not α/β.

questions.question: Fructose in solution predominantly forms which ring type?
questions.explanation: Fructose closes on itself to form a furanose (five-membered) ring.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Pyranose is the six-membered form, typical of glucose.
Correct. Fructose forms a furanose ring.
Incorrect. The open-chain form is a minor fraction.
Incorrect. Fructose does not form a bicyclic structure.

questions.question: In fructose, the anomeric carbon is:
questions.explanation: Fructose is a ketose; the ketone carbon is C2, so C2 is the anomeric carbon.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. C1 is the anomeric carbon of aldoses like glucose.
Correct. In fructose the ketone is at C2.
Incorrect. C5 is the ring oxygen-bearing carbon.
Incorrect. C6 is a terminal CH2OH.
questions.hint: The anomeric carbon is the carbonyl carbon.

questions.question: Reducing sugars are defined in the lecture as sugars that:
options: React with a basic Cu2+ solution (Benedict's reagent) to form a red-orange precipitate of Cu2O
Do not react with Benedict's reagent
questions.explanation: Sugars with a free hemiacetal react with Benedict's reagent (basic Cu2+) to form a red-orange precipitate of Cu2O and are called reducing sugars.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the definition of reducing sugars.
Incorrect. Non-reacting sugars are non-reducing sugars.
Incorrect. Ketoses can also reduce.
Incorrect. All monosaccharides are reducing sugars.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about monosaccharides and Benedict's reagent is correct?
options: Monosaccharides do not react with Benedict's reagent
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly states that all monosaccharides are reducing sugars.
optionExplanations: Correct. All monosaccharides reduce Benedict's reagent.
Incorrect. Aldoses are also reducing sugars.
Incorrect. They react to give a red-orange precipitate.
Incorrect. Pentoses and trioses also reduce.
questions.hint: All monosaccharides contain a free hemiacetal.

questions.question: Oxidation of the aldehyde carbon (C1) of glucose produces:
questions.explanation: Oxidation at C1 (the aldehyde carbon) of glucose gives gluconic acid.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucuronic acid results from oxidation at C6.
Correct. C1 oxidation gives gluconic acid.
Incorrect. Glucaric acid results from oxidation at both C1 and C6.
Incorrect. Sorbitol is a reduction product, not an oxidation product.

questions.question: Oxidation of the terminal CH2OH carbon (C6) of glucose produces:
questions.explanation: Oxidation at C6 of glucose produces glucuronic acid.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Gluconic acid results from C1 oxidation.
Correct. C6 oxidation gives glucuronic acid.
Incorrect. Glucaric acid results from oxidation at both ends.
Incorrect. Galactose is a C4 epimer, not an oxidation product.

questions.question: Which product forms when both C1 and C6 of glucose are oxidized?
questions.explanation: Oxidation at both ends of glucose yields glucaric acid.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Gluconic acid arises only from C1 oxidation.
Incorrect. Glucuronic acid arises only from C6 oxidation.
Correct. Glucaric acid = oxidation at both C1 and C6.
Incorrect. Glucose 6-phosphate is a phosphate ester, not an oxidation product.

questions.question: Phosphate esters of monosaccharides typically form at which carbon of aldohexoses according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that phosphate esters can form at the 6-carbon of aldohexoses and aldoketoses (e.g., glucose 6-phosphate, fructose 6-phosphate).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. C1 is the anomeric carbon.
Incorrect. C2 is the anomeric carbon for ketoses.
Correct. C6 is the phosphate ester site.
Incorrect. C4 is the site of the glucose/galactose epimer difference.
questions.hint: The phosphate attaches to the terminal CH2OH.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a place where phosphate esters of monosaccharides are found according to the lecture?
options: Sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA and RNA
The lipid bilayer of cell membranes
questions.explanation: The lecture lists DNA/RNA backbones, ATP, and metabolic intermediates as sites where monosaccharide phosphate esters occur, not membrane lipids.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. DNA/RNA backbones are listed.
Incorrect. ATP is listed.
Incorrect. Metabolic intermediates are listed.
Correct. Membrane lipids are not listed in this context.
questions.hint: Which option is unrelated to nucleotides or metabolism?

questions.question: A glycosidic linkage is best described as:
options: The new carbon-oxygen bond formed when the hemiacetal/hemiketal of a sugar reacts with an alcohol
A peptide bond between two amino acids
A carbon-carbon bond between two monosaccharides
An ester bond between a fatty acid and glycerol
questions.explanation: The lecture defines the glycosidic linkage as the new carbon-oxygen bond formed between the anomeric carbon and the alcohol oxygen.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the lecture's definition.
Incorrect. Peptide bonds are in proteins.
Incorrect. Glycosidic bonds are C–O, not C–C.
Incorrect. That describes a triglyceride.
questions.hint: It involves the anomeric carbon and an oxygen.

questions.question: Which of the following is true of glycosides?
options: They are reducing sugars because their ring can open
They cannot reduce Benedict's reagent because the ring can no longer open to the open-chain form
They always have a free anomeric carbon
questions.explanation: Once a glycoside is formed, the ring can no longer open to the open-chain form, so glycosides are not reducing sugars and do not react with Cu2+.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glycosides are not reducing sugars.
Correct. Ring-opening is blocked, so no reduction occurs.
Incorrect. Glycosides are not limited to ketones.
Incorrect. The anomeric carbon is involved in the glycosidic bond, not free.

questions.question: When α-D-glucose reacts with methanol under acid catalysis, the product is:
questions.explanation: The hemiacetal of α-D-glucose reacts with methanol under acid catalysis to give methyl α-D-glucopyranoside, a glycoside.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the glycoside formed with methanol.
Incorrect. Gluconic acid is an oxidation product.
Incorrect. Phosphate esters use phosphoric acid, not methanol.
Incorrect. Sorbitol is a reduction product.

questions.question: Maltose is composed of:
options: α-D-glucose and β-D-fructose joined by α-1,β-2 linkage
Two α-D-glucose units joined by an α(1→4) glycosidic linkage
β-D-galactose and α-D-glucose joined by a β(1→4) linkage
questions.explanation: The lecture describes maltose as two α-D-glucose units linked by an α(1→4) glycosidic linkage.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That describes sucrose.
Correct. Maltose = glucose + glucose (α-1,4).
Incorrect. That describes lactose.
Incorrect. That describes hyaluronic acid repeating units.

questions.question: Lactose is composed of:
options: Two glucose units joined by an α(1→4) linkage
Glucose and fructose joined by α-1,β-2 linkage
β-D-galactose and α-D-glucose joined by a β(1→4) linkage
Sulfated glucuronic acid and sulfated glucosamine
questions.explanation: Lactose consists of β-D-galactose linked to α-D-glucose by a β(1→4) glycosidic linkage.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That is maltose.
Incorrect. That is sucrose.
Correct. Lactose = galactose + glucose (β-1,4).
Incorrect. That describes heparin.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about sucrose is correct according to the lecture?
options: Both anomeric carbons of glucose and fructose are involved in the glycosidic linkage, so sucrose is not a reducing sugar
Sucrose is composed of two galactose units
Sucrose contains a free anomeric carbon on glucose
questions.explanation: The lecture states that both anomeric carbons of glucose and fructose are tied together in the glycosidic linkage, so neither ring can open and sucrose is not a reducing sugar.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Sucrose is not a reducing sugar.
Correct. Both anomeric carbons are locked in the glycosidic bond.
Incorrect. Sucrose is glucose + fructose.
Incorrect. The glucose anomeric carbon is involved in the glycosidic bond.

questions.question: Raffinose is described in the lecture as:
options: An oligosaccharide found in peas and beans, largely undigested until reaching intestinal flora
A polysaccharide made of glucose and galactose
A disaccharide composed of glucose and fructose
questions.explanation: Raffinose is an oligosaccharide found in peas and beans; it is largely undigested until reaching the intestinal flora in the large intestine, releasing hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. It is not a milk monosaccharide.
Correct. This matches the lecture.
Incorrect. It is an oligosaccharide, not a polysaccharide.
Incorrect. Sucrose is glucose + fructose; raffinose contains galactose, glucose, and fructose.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes amylose from amylopectin?
options: Amylose is branched; amylopectin is unbranched
Amylose is unbranched with α(1→4) linkages; amylopectin has α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches
Both are entirely made of β(1→4) linkages
Both are made of fructose units
questions.explanation: Amylose consists of long unbranched chains of glucose with α(1→4) linkages; amylopectin has α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches every 24–30 glucose units.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The branching pattern is reversed.
Correct. This matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Cellulose uses β(1→4) linkages, not starch components.
Incorrect. Starch is made of glucose, not fructose.

questions.question: Approximately what percentage of plant starch is amylose?
questions.explanation: The lecture states 10%–20% of plant starch is amylose, with 80%–90% being amylopectin.
optionExplanations: Correct. Amylose = 10%–20% of plant starch.
Incorrect. This range is not stated.
Incorrect. This range is more consistent with amylopectin.
Incorrect. Plant starch is not 90%–100% amylose.

questions.question: Which starch component gives a deep blue-purple color with iodine?
options: Amylose, because its helices trap iodine molecules
questions.explanation: Amylose helices can trap iodine molecules, forming a characteristic deep blue-purple color.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The iodine color test is attributed to amylose.
Correct. Iodine trapped inside amylose helices gives the color.
Incorrect. Cellulose does not give this characteristic color.
Incorrect. Glycogen gives a different (reddish-brown) color with iodine.

questions.question: Which statement about glycogen is correct according to the lecture?
options: Glycogen is a starch found in plants with α(1→4) and α(1→6) linkages
Glycogen is structurally similar to amylopectin but more highly branched, with branches every 8–12 glucose units
Glycogen is a polymer of fructose found in the liver
questions.explanation: Glycogen is structurally similar to amylopectin but is even more highly branched (every 8–12 glucose units) and is abundant in liver and muscle.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glycogen is the animal starch, not a plant starch.
Correct. This matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Glycogen is a polymer of glucose, not fructose.
Incorrect. Glycogen uses α linkages, not β.
questions.hint: Animal starch with denser branching than amylopectin.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about cellulose?
options: Cellulose is a branched polymer of glucose with α(1→4) and α(1→6) linkages
Cellulose is an unbranched polymer of D-glucose with β(1→4) glycosidic linkages
Cellulose is a polymer of fructose linked by α(1→4) bonds
Cellulose is a heteropolysaccharide of aminosugars and uronic acids
questions.explanation: Cellulose consists of long unbranched chains of D-glucose connected by β(1→4) glycosidic linkages (300–3000 glucose units per molecule).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That describes amylopectin/glycogen.
Correct. Cellulose = unbranched glucose + β(1→4) linkages.
Incorrect. Cellulose contains glucose, not fructose.
Incorrect. That describes heteropolysaccharides.
questions.hint: β-linkages give cellulose its rigid structure.

questions.question: Which statement about heteropolysaccharides (mucopolysaccharides) is correct?
options: They contain only glucose units linked by α(1→4) bonds
They are long, unbranched chains of repeating disaccharides composed of amino sugars and uronic acids
They are made exclusively of monosaccharides joined by β(1→4) bonds
They are insoluble in water and provide no lubrication
questions.explanation: The lecture defines heteropolysaccharides as long unbranched chains of repeating disaccharide units composed of amino sugars and uronic acids.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That describes starch, not heteropolysaccharides.
Correct. This is the definition from the lecture.
Incorrect. Not all heteropolysaccharides use β(1→4) linkages.
Incorrect. They attract water, forming viscous mucus and acting as lubricants.

questions.question: Hyaluronic acid is composed of which repeating disaccharide unit?
options: Sulfated glucuronic acid and sulfated glucosamine joined by α-1,4 bonds
D-glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine joined by β-1,3 bonds
Glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine joined by β-1,3 bonds
Two glucose units joined by α(1→4) bonds
questions.explanation: Hyaluronic acid is a repeating disaccharide of D-glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine joined by β-1,3 bonds; it acts as a lubricant and shock absorbent in joints.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That describes heparin.
Correct. Hyaluronic acid = glucuronic acid + N-acetylglucosamine (β-1,3).
Incorrect. That describes chondroitin.
Incorrect. Hyaluronic acid contains amino sugars and uronic acids.
questions.hint: Found in joints as a lubricant.

questions.question: Heparin is composed of which repeating disaccharide unit, and what is its main biological function?
options: Sulfated glucuronic acid and sulfated glucosamine joined by α-1,4 bonds; acts as an anticoagulant
D-glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine joined by β-1,3 bonds; acts as a lubricant
Glucose and galactose joined by β-1,4 bonds; acts as an anticoagulant
Two fructose units joined by α-1,2 bonds; acts as a shock absorber
questions.explanation: Heparin is made of sulfated glucuronic acid and sulfated glucosamine joined by α-1,4 bonds; it is used as an anticoagulant.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the lecture.
Incorrect. That describes chondroitin.
Incorrect. Lactose is glucose + galactose (β-1,4), not an anticoagulant.
Incorrect. Fructose does not make up heparin.

questions.question: Chondroitin is composed of which repeating disaccharide unit?
options: Glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine joined by β-1,3 bonds
Sulfated glucuronic acid and sulfated glucosamine joined by α-1,4 bonds
D-glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine joined by β-1,3 bonds
Two glucose units joined by α-1,6 bonds
questions.explanation: Chondroitin is composed of glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine joined by β-1,3 bonds; it is found in bone, cartilage, tendons, ligaments, and aorta.
optionExplanations: Correct. Chondroitin = glucuronic acid + N-acetylgalactosamine (β-1,3).
Incorrect. That describes heparin.
Incorrect. That describes hyaluronic acid.
Incorrect. That describes a branch point in amylopectin, not chondroitin.
questions.hint: Found in cartilage and connective tissue.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the structural role of heteropolysaccharides when bound to proteins?
options: They lose their ability to attract water
They form glycoproteins and, because of charged groups, attract large amounts of water to produce viscous mucous secretions, acting as lubricants
questions.explanation: Heteropolysaccharides bind to proteins to form glycoproteins; charged groups attract water, producing viscous mucous secretions that act as lubricants (hence the name mucopolysaccharides).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They attract water.
Correct. This matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Glycoproteins are not classified as reducing sugars.
Incorrect. Cellulose is a plant homo-polysaccharide.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a hexose?
questions.explanation: Ribose is a pentose (5 carbons); glucose, fructose, and galactose are all hexoses (6 carbons).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose is a hexose.
Incorrect. Fructose is a hexose.
Incorrect. Galactose is a hexose.
Correct. Ribose is a pentose, not a hexose.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between carbohydrates and the term 'saccharide'?
options: Saccharide is an obsolete term no longer used in biochemistry
Saccharide is a synonym for carbohydrate, derived from the Greek word for sugar
Saccharide refers only to the sugar portion of a glycoprotein
questions.explanation: The lecture states that carbohydrates are also called saccharides, from the Greek 'saccharo' meaning sugar.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Saccharide is still commonly used.
Correct. Saccharide = sugar (Greek).
Incorrect. Saccharide covers all carbohydrate classes.
Incorrect. Saccharide is a general term, not restricted to glycoproteins.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes monosaccharides from oligosaccharides?
options: Monosaccharides are polymers; oligosaccharides are monomers
Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolyzed into smaller sugars; oligosaccharides yield 3–10 monosaccharides on hydrolysis
Oligosaccharides are found only in animals
questions.explanation: Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates (cannot be hydrolyzed further), while oligosaccharides give 3–10 monosaccharide units on hydrolysis.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The two classes are reversed.
Correct. Monosaccharides = simplest; oligosaccharides = 3–10 units.
Incorrect. Carbon numbers vary by class.
Incorrect. Oligosaccharides like raffinose are found in plants.

questions.question: Which of the following biological roles of carbohydrates is NOT explicitly listed in the lecture?
options: Forming part of the structures of some cells and tissues
Serving as coenzymes for redox reactions
Acting as a form of stored chemical energy
questions.explanation: The lecture lists energy through oxidation, carbon supply, stored chemical energy, and structural roles; coenzyme function is not among them.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Energy through oxidation is listed.
Incorrect. Structural roles are listed.
Correct. Coenzyme function is not listed.
Incorrect. Stored chemical energy is listed.
questions.hint: Which role belongs to vitamins rather than carbohydrates?

questions.question: Which statement about the classification of monosaccharides by carbon number is correct?
options: A tetrose has 6 carbons and a hexose has 4 carbons
A triose has 3 carbons, a tetrose has 4, a pentose has 5, and a hexose has 6
questions.explanation: The lecture lists trioses (3 C), tetroses (4 C), pentoses (5 C), and hexoses (6 C).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The numbers are reversed.
Correct. Matches the classification table.
Incorrect. Monosaccharides range from 3 to 6 carbons and beyond.
Incorrect. Trioses can be aldoses (glyceraldehyde) or ketoses (dihydroxyacetone).
questions.hint: Match prefixes: tri = 3, tetr = 4, pent = 5, hex = 6.

questions.question: Dihydroxyacetone is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Dihydroxyacetone has three carbons and a ketone group, so it is a ketose triose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. It is a ketose, not an aldose.
Correct. Ketose + 3 carbons.
Incorrect. It has 3 carbons, not 4.
Incorrect. It has 3 carbons, not 6.
questions.hint: How many carbons and which functional group?

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an aldose tetrose?
questions.explanation: The lecture's classification table lists erythrose as the aldose tetrose example.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glyceraldehyde is a triose.
Correct. Erythrose is the aldose tetrose.
Incorrect. Ribose is a pentose.
Incorrect. Glucose is a hexose.

questions.question: Which property distinguishes a ketose from an aldose?
options: The presence of a ketone carbonyl versus an aldehyde carbonyl
The type of ring formed in solution
questions.explanation: Aldoses contain an aldehyde group; ketoses contain a ketone group, per the lecture's classification rule (aldo- vs keto-).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Chiral carbon count varies by carbon number.
Correct. Aldose vs ketose is defined by the carbonyl type.
Incorrect. Optical rotation direction is not related to aldo/keto.
Incorrect. Ring type depends on sugar identity, not aldo/keto classification directly.
questions.hint: Look at the carbonyl functional group.

questions.question: A molecule of 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid has how many chiral carbons and how many stereoisomers (maximum)?
questions.explanation: Each central carbon is attached to four different groups and is chiral; 2^2 = 4 possible stereoisomers.
optionExplanations: Correct. 2 chiral carbons give 2^2 = 4 stereoisomers.
Incorrect. Two carbons are chiral here.
Incorrect. Only two carbons are chiral.
Incorrect. Both central carbons are chiral.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE about chiral molecules?
options: They have identical physical properties to their enantiomers except for the direction of polarized light rotation
They have completely different melting points from their enantiomers
They have no relationship to their mirror images
questions.explanation: Enantiomers have identical melting points, boiling points, and refractive indices; they differ only in the direction of polarized light rotation and in biological interactions.
optionExplanations: Correct. Only optical rotation and biological interactions differ.
Incorrect. Melting points are identical for enantiomers.
Incorrect. Many chiral molecules are biologically active.
Incorrect. Chirality implies a mirror-image relationship.

questions.question: Which set contains only molecules that are typically chiral?
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly lists hands, gloves, and shoes as chiral objects and drinking glasses, spheres, and cubes as achiral.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Those are achiral.
Correct. Hands, gloves, shoes are chiral examples.
Incorrect. Those molecules are achiral.
Incorrect. Those are geometric shapes, not chiral molecules.
questions.hint: Which set has mirror-image forms that cannot be superimposed?

questions.question: How many chiral carbons are present in a molecule with 2^4 = 16 maximum stereoisomers?
questions.explanation: 2^n = 16 means n = 4 chiral carbons.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. 2^2 = 4.
Incorrect. 2^3 = 8.
Correct. 2^4 = 16.
Incorrect. 2^5 = 32.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes an asymmetric carbon?
options: A carbon bonded to four identical atoms
A carbon bonded to four different groups
A carbon in a double bond
questions.explanation: An asymmetric (chiral) carbon is bonded to four different groups.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Four identical groups would be achiral (e.g., CH4).
Correct. Four different groups = chiral.
Incorrect. Double-bonded carbons are not chiral centers.
Incorrect. CH2Cl2 has no hydrogens on one carbon yet is achiral.
questions.hint: All four groups must be different.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Fischer projections is correct?
options: Horizontal bonds point away from the viewer and vertical bonds point toward the viewer
Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds point away from the viewer
All bonds lie in the plane of the paper
The carbonyl group is placed at the bottom and the CH2OH is at the top
questions.explanation: In a Fischer projection, horizontal bonds point toward the viewer, vertical bonds point away; the carbonyl is placed at or near the top and CH2OH at the bottom.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The directions are reversed.
Correct. Horizontal = toward; vertical = away.
Incorrect. The projection represents a 3D molecule in 2D.
Incorrect. The carbonyl is at the top, CH2OH at the bottom.

questions.question: In the D-family of monosaccharides, the OH group on the reference (farthest) chiral carbon is oriented to the:
options: Right when the carbonyl is drawn at the top
Left when the carbonyl is drawn at the top
questions.explanation: The D-isomer has the OH group on the reference chiral carbon pointing right when the carbonyl is at the top.
optionExplanations: Correct. D = OH right.
Incorrect. OH left corresponds to L.
Incorrect. 'Top' is where the carbonyl is.
Incorrect. 'Bottom' is where CH2OH is.

questions.question: How is the D- or L- configuration of a monosaccharide determined?
options: By the direction of polarized light rotation
By the position of the OH group on the anomeric carbon
By the position of the OH group on the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl
By the number of carbons in the chain
questions.explanation: The D/L designation is based on the configuration at the chiral carbon farthest from the carbonyl group.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Optical rotation direction is not the same as D/L.
Incorrect. The anomeric carbon determines α/β, not D/L.
Correct. Farthest chiral carbon determines D/L.
Incorrect. Carbon number is unrelated to D/L.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE about the relationship between D/L configuration and optical activity (+/−)?
options: D/L designation and the direction of optical rotation are independent properties
Optical rotation is determined by the number of chiral carbons only
questions.explanation: D/L is a configurational descriptor based on the reference chiral carbon; the direction of optical rotation (+ or −) is a separate experimental property.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Some D-sugars are levorotatory (e.g., D-fructose).
Incorrect. Not all L-sugars are levorotatory.
Correct. They are independent properties.
Incorrect. Rotation direction is determined by the whole molecule's structure, not just the count.

questions.question: A solution of an unknown sugar rotates plane-polarized light to the left. This sugar is:
questions.explanation: Levorotatory (−) substances rotate plane-polarized light to the left.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Dextrorotatory rotates right.
Correct. Left rotation = levorotatory.
Incorrect. A racemic mixture is optically inactive.
Incorrect. Optically inactive means no rotation.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about a racemic mixture?
options: It consists of only one enantiomer
It consists of equal amounts of two enantiomers and is optically inactive
It always rotates light to the right
questions.explanation: A racemate contains equal quantities of two enantiomers whose rotatory effects cancel, making the mixture optically inactive.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. A racemate contains both enantiomers.
Correct. Equal amounts → no net rotation.
Incorrect. Racemates are optically inactive.
Incorrect. Racemates contain chiral molecules.

questions.question: A pair of enantiomers has the same:
options: Biological activity in a chiral environment
Interaction with an enzyme active site
questions.explanation: Enantiomers have identical physical constants (melting point, boiling point, refraction) but differ in optical rotation direction and in interactions with other chiral environments (like enzyme active sites).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They rotate light in opposite directions.
Incorrect. Biological activity often differs dramatically.
Correct. Melting points are identical.
Incorrect. Enzyme interactions can differ (e.g., thalidomide).

questions.question: Which of the following monosaccharides is the sweetest, as stated in the lecture?
questions.explanation: Fructose is the sweetest of the monosaccharides, about 73% sweeter than sucrose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose is less sweet than fructose.
Correct. Fructose is the sweetest.
Incorrect. Galactose is less sweet.
Incorrect. Sucrose is a disaccharide and is less sweet than fructose.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about the solubility of monosaccharides?
options: They are insoluble in water due to their high molecular weights
Their many OH groups make them much more water soluble than molecules of similar molecular weight
They dissolve only in nonpolar solvents
questions.explanation: The many OH groups in monosaccharides make them highly water soluble; glucose, for instance, dissolves 1 g per 1 mL of water forming a syrup.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They are highly soluble in water.
Correct. Many OH groups → high water solubility.
Incorrect. They are water-soluble, not nonpolar-soluble.
Incorrect. Solubility generally increases with temperature.

questions.question: Monosaccharides in aqueous solution predominantly exist as:
questions.explanation: In solution, monosaccharides exist primarily as cyclic hemiacetals (aldoses) or hemiketals (ketoses) formed by intramolecular attack of an OH on the carbonyl group.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Only a tiny fraction remains as the open-chain form.
Correct. Cyclic forms dominate in solution.
Incorrect. Monosaccharides are not fully ionized.
Incorrect. Crystal form does not describe solution behavior.

questions.question: The reaction that converts an open-chain monosaccharide into a cyclic hemiacetal involves:
options: Attack of a hydroxyl group on the carbonyl carbon
Loss of water from two hydroxyl groups only
Oxidation of the aldehyde to an acid
questions.explanation: An alcohol (OH) group in the same molecule attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a stable cyclic hemiacetal (or hemiketal for ketoses).
optionExplanations: Correct. Intramolecular OH attack on the carbonyl.
Incorrect. Water loss is not the essential step here.
Incorrect. Phosphorylation is a separate reaction.
Incorrect. Oxidation produces acids like gluconic acid.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes the anomeric carbon?
options: It is the terminal CH2OH carbon
It is the carbon derived from the carbonyl carbon upon cyclization
It is always achiral in cyclic sugars
It is not involved in glycosidic bond formation
questions.explanation: The anomeric carbon is the carbonyl carbon that becomes a new chiral center on cyclization, giving α and β forms.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The CH2OH is at the other end.
Correct. This is the definition of the anomeric carbon.
Incorrect. It is a chiral center.
Incorrect. Glycosidic bonds form at the anomeric carbon.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about α- and β-anomers?
options: They differ only in the position of the OH group on the anomeric carbon
They are enantiomers of each other
They have different numbers of carbons
They can never interconvert in solution
questions.explanation: α and β anomers differ only in the orientation of the OH group on the anomeric carbon; they readily interconvert in solution via the open-chain form (mutarotation).
optionExplanations: Correct. Difference is only at C1.
Incorrect. They are diastereomers, not enantiomers.
Incorrect. Carbon count is identical.
Incorrect. They interconvert in solution.

questions.question: Which of the following rings is a furanose?
questions.explanation: A furanose is a five-membered ring containing one oxygen; a pyranose is a six-membered ring.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That is a pyranose.
Correct. Five-membered = furanose.
Incorrect. That would be an epoxide-type ring.
Incorrect. That would be an oxepane-type ring.

questions.question: Which type of sugar usually forms a furanose ring?
options: Aldopentoses such as ribose only in RNA
questions.explanation: Fructose, a ketohexose, closes on itself to form a furanose ring; glucose (an aldohexose) forms a pyranose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Aldohexoses typically form pyranose rings.
Correct. Fructose forms a furanose.
Incorrect. Ribose in RNA forms a furanose but the question is about which type of sugar does so as its major ring.
Incorrect. Not all monosaccharides form furanose rings.
questions.hint: Which ketose is present in honey?

questions.question: A reducing sugar is best defined as one that:
options: Has a free hemiacetal that can reduce Cu2+ in Benedict's reagent
questions.explanation: Reducing sugars have a free hemiacetal at the anomeric carbon, which reduces Cu2+ (Benedict's reagent) to Cu2O (red-orange precipitate).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Ketoses can also be reducing.
Correct. Free hemiacetal = reducing sugar.
Incorrect. Reducing sugars react with oxidizing agents.
Incorrect. All sugars have OH groups.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds is NOT a reducing sugar?
questions.explanation: Sucrose is not a reducing sugar because both anomeric carbons (glucose and fructose) are locked in the glycosidic linkage, preventing ring-opening.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose is reducing.
Incorrect. Fructose is reducing.
Incorrect. Maltose has a free hemiacetal on one glucose unit.
Correct. Sucrose is non-reducing.
questions.hint: Which one has both anomeric carbons locked?

questions.question: What is the product when the aldehyde carbon of glucose is oxidized but the terminal CH2OH is not?
questions.explanation: Oxidation of only the aldehyde carbon (C1) produces gluconic acid; oxidation of only C6 produces glucuronic acid; oxidation of both produces glucaric acid.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucaric acid comes from oxidation at both C1 and C6.
Correct. C1-only oxidation gives gluconic acid.
Incorrect. Glucuronic acid comes from C6-only oxidation.
Incorrect. Sorbitol is a reduction product.

questions.question: Which enzyme-related reaction product is derived from oxidizing C6 of glucose and is used in detoxification and connective tissue synthesis?
questions.explanation: Glucuronic acid, produced by oxidation of C6, is used in detoxification reactions and is a component of connective tissue polysaccharides.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Gluconic acid arises from C1 oxidation.
Correct. Glucuronic acid is used in detoxification and connective tissue.
Incorrect. Glucaric acid comes from oxidation at both ends.
Incorrect. Sorbitol is a reduction product.

questions.question: Phosphate esters of monosaccharides are important in all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA and RNA
questions.explanation: The lecture lists DNA/RNA backbones, ATP, and metabolic intermediates; phosphorylation is not directly part of ribosomal protein synthesis.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. DNA/RNA backbones are listed.
Incorrect. ATP is listed.
Incorrect. Metabolic intermediates are listed.
Correct. Ribosomal protein synthesis is a different process.
questions.hint: Which option is not related to phosphate esters?

questions.question: The formation of a glycoside from a sugar and an alcohol:
options: Increases the number of free anomeric carbons
Converts a reducing sugar into a non-reducing sugar
questions.explanation: Formation of a glycosidic bond locks the anomeric carbon into a full acetal/ketal, so the ring can no longer open; the resulting glycoside is non-reducing.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. It removes the free anomeric carbon.
Correct. Glycosides are non-reducing.
Incorrect. Glycoside formation is not an oxidation.
Incorrect. Acid catalysis is typically required.
questions.hint: The ring can no longer open.

questions.question: Which of the following disaccharides has both anomeric carbons involved in the glycosidic bond?
questions.explanation: In sucrose, both anomeric carbons (of glucose and fructose) participate in the glycosidic linkage, so it is non-reducing.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Maltose has a free anomeric carbon on one glucose.
Incorrect. Lactose has a free anomeric carbon on glucose.
Correct. Sucrose has both anomeric carbons locked.
Incorrect. Cellobiose has a free hemiacetal.
questions.hint: Which one is not a reducing sugar?

questions.question: When sucrose is hydrolyzed under acidic conditions, the products are:
questions.explanation: Acid hydrolysis of sucrose yields glucose and fructose; this mixture is called invert sugar and is sweeter than sucrose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That is maltose hydrolysis.
Incorrect. That is lactose hydrolysis.
Correct. Sucrose → glucose + fructose (invert sugar).
Incorrect. Sucrose does not contain galactose.
questions.hint: Sucrose is made of glucose and fructose.

questions.question: Which statement about the sweetness of invert sugar is correct?
options: Invert sugar is less sweet than sucrose
Invert sugar is sweeter than sucrose due to its fructose content
Invert sugar has the same sweetness as sucrose
questions.explanation: Invert sugar — the acid-hydrolysis product of sucrose — is sweeter than sucrose because of the fructose released.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. It is sweeter, not less sweet.
Correct. Fructose makes invert sugar sweeter.
Incorrect. Sweetness differs.
Incorrect. Invert sugar is sweet.

questions.question: Caramel is best described as:
options: A mixture of monosaccharides formed by enzyme hydrolysis of starch
The solid residue formed from heating sucrose
questions.explanation: The lecture states that caramel is the solid residue formed from heating sucrose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Caramel is not an enzymatic product.
Correct. Caramel = heated sucrose residue.
Incorrect. Caramel is not a disaccharide.
Incorrect. Raffinose is the pea oligosaccharide.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about maltose?
options: It is produced during the germination of grains and during starch digestion
It consists of galactose and glucose
It contains a β(1→4) glycosidic linkage
questions.explanation: Maltose (malt sugar) is produced in germinating grain as starch is broken down during malting, and it also forms during starch hydrolysis to glucose in digestion.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Maltose is a reducing sugar.
Correct. Maltose is produced during germination and starch digestion.
Incorrect. Maltose = glucose + glucose.
Incorrect. Maltose uses α(1→4) linkage.

questions.question: Which disaccharide is digested by the enzyme lactase?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that lactose is digested by the enzyme lactase; lactose intolerance results from reduced lactase activity.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Maltose is digested by maltase.
Incorrect. Sucrose is digested by sucrase.
Correct. Lactose is digested by lactase.
Incorrect. Cellobiose is not a major dietary disaccharide.
questions.hint: The enzyme name matches the sugar name.

questions.question: Raffinose is best classified as:
options: An oligosaccharide found in peas and beans
A polysaccharide made of glucose and galactose
A disaccharide made of glucose and fructose
questions.explanation: Raffinose is an oligosaccharide found in peas and beans, containing galactose, glucose, and fructose units.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. It is not a milk monosaccharide.
Correct. Raffinose is an oligosaccharide in legumes.
Incorrect. It is an oligosaccharide, not a polysaccharide.
Incorrect. Raffinose has three sugar units.
questions.hint: Legumes cause gas due to this sugar.

questions.question: Why does eating beans cause flatulence according to the lecture?
options: Raffinose is largely undigested until reaching intestinal flora, which release hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane
Beans contain cellulose that humans digest
Beans contain amylose that ferments in the stomach
questions.explanation: Raffinose from peas and beans is largely undigested until it reaches the intestinal flora in the large intestine, where it is fermented, releasing hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose is not the source of gas.
Correct. Raffinose fermentation causes flatulence.
Incorrect. Humans cannot digest cellulose.
Incorrect. Amylose is digested by human enzymes.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the difference between amylose and amylopectin?
options: Amylose is branched; amylopectin is unbranched
Amylose is unbranched with α(1→4) linkages; amylopectin has α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branches
Both are made entirely of β(1→4) linkages
Both are found in animal tissues
questions.explanation: Amylose is a long unbranched chain of glucose linked by α(1→4) bonds; amylopectin has α(1→4) chains with α(1→6) branch points every 24–30 glucose units.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Branching is reversed.
Correct. Matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Cellulose, not starch, uses β(1→4).
Incorrect. Both are plant polysaccharides; glycogen is animal.

questions.question: Which polysaccharide is described as 'animal starch'?
questions.explanation: Glycogen is also known as animal starch; it is stored in the liver and muscles and is highly branched.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Amylose is a plant starch component.
Incorrect. Amylopectin is a plant starch component.
Correct. Glycogen = animal starch.
Incorrect. Cellulose is structural in plants.

questions.question: The branching frequency in glycogen (every 8–12 glucose units) compared with amylopectin (every 24–30 glucose units) means that:
options: Glycogen is less branched than amylopectin
Glycogen is more highly branched than amylopectin
Both have the same degree of branching
questions.explanation: Because branches occur more frequently in glycogen, glycogen is more highly branched than amylopectin; this allows rapid mobilization of glucose when needed.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glycogen is more branched.
Correct. Every 8–12 units vs every 24–30 units.
Incorrect. The frequencies differ.
Incorrect. Branching affects the speed of glucose release.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about glycogen is correct?
options: Glycogen is a polymer of fructose
Glycogen is abundant in liver and muscles and on hydrolysis gives D-glucose
questions.explanation: Glycogen is abundant in the liver and muscles; on hydrolysis it forms D-glucose, which maintains blood sugar levels and provides energy.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glycogen uses α(1→4) and α(1→6) linkages.
Incorrect. Glycogen is made of glucose, not fructose.
Correct. Matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Glycogen is a homopolysaccharide.
questions.hint: Where is glycogen stored, and what does it yield?

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes cellulose from amylose?
options: Cellulose is branched; amylose is unbranched
Cellulose uses β(1→4) linkages and is straight-chained; amylose uses α(1→4) linkages and can form helices
Cellulose contains fructose; amylose contains glucose
questions.explanation: Cellulose's β(1→4) linkages give it extended straight chains with rigid hydrogen bonding, whereas amylose's α(1→4) linkages allow helical coiling.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Cellulose is unbranched.
Correct. β vs α linkages, straight vs helical.
Incorrect. Both are glucose polymers.
Incorrect. Only amylose is digestible by humans.

questions.question: Which is the single most abundant organic compound on Earth, as stated in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that cellulose is the most important structural polysaccharide and the single most abundant organic compound on Earth; wood is 50% cellulose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Starch is abundant but not the most abundant.
Incorrect. Glycogen is stored in animals and is less abundant overall.
Correct. Cellulose is the most abundant organic compound.
Incorrect. Hyaluronic acid is a heteropolysaccharide found in connective tissue.

questions.question: Which statement about cellulose digestion in animals is correct?
options: All animals can digest cellulose using their own enzymes
Most animals lack the enzymes to digest cellulose, but ruminants use symbiotic bacteria
Cellulose is fully absorbed without digestion
Cellulose is digested by pancreatic amylase
questions.explanation: Most animals cannot digest cellulose due to lack of β-glucosidase enzymes; ruminants (cows, sheep, goats) rely on symbiotic gut bacteria that break down cellulose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Most animals lack the required enzymes.
Correct. Ruminants use bacteria to digest cellulose.
Incorrect. Cellulose is not absorbed intact.
Incorrect. Amylase cannot hydrolyze β-linkages.

questions.question: How does cellulose provide nutritional benefit to humans even though we cannot digest it?
options: It acts as roughage (dietary fiber), stimulating intestinal contraction and helping food pass through the digestive system
It is converted to glucose in the liver
It acts as an enzyme cofactor
questions.explanation: Cellulose provides roughage (dietary fiber), stimulating intestinal contractions and helping food pass through the digestive system.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Human enzymes cannot break cellulose down for energy.
Correct. Roughage stimulates digestion.
Incorrect. Cellulose is not converted to glucose in humans.
Incorrect. Cellulose is not an enzyme cofactor.

questions.question: Which of the following industrial products is derived from cellulose according to the lecture?
options: Wood, paper, cotton, cellophane, rayon, and nitrocellulose
questions.explanation: The lecture lists wood, paper, cotton, cellophane, rayon, linen, nitrocellulose (guncotton), and photographic films (cellulose acetate) as cellulose-derived industrial products.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Insulin is a protein hormone.
Correct. All are cellulose-derived.
Incorrect. Aspirin is a synthetic drug.
Incorrect. Vitamin C is a water-soluble vitamin.

questions.question: Heteropolysaccharides are also called mucopolysaccharides because:
options: They produce viscous mucous secretions and act as lubricants due to their charged groups attracting water
questions.explanation: Because of the presence of charged groups, heteropolysaccharides attract large amounts of water, producing viscous mucous secretions, hence the name mucopolysaccharides.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. 'Muco' relates to mucus, not muscle.
Correct. Charged groups attract water → mucous secretions.
Incorrect. They contain amino sugars and uronic acids.
Incorrect. Color is not relevant.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a heteropolysaccharide with its biological function?
options: Chondroitin — component of bone, cartilage, tendons, ligaments, and aorta
questions.explanation: Chondroitin is found in bone, cartilage, tendons, ligaments, and aorta; hyaluronic acid is the joint lubricant; heparin is the anticoagulant.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Hyaluronic acid is a joint lubricant.
Incorrect. Heparin is an anticoagulant.
Correct. Chondroitin is found in connective tissues.
Incorrect. Cellulose is a structural plant polysaccharide.
questions.hint: Match the molecule to its tissue or function.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains why carbohydrates are called 'biomolecules'?
options: They are only found in non-living matter
They are closely associated with living organisms and include carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids
They are only synthesized in the laboratory
questions.explanation: The lecture groups carbohydrates with lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids as biomolecules because they are closely associated with living organisms.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They are found in living organisms.
Correct. This is the definition given in the lecture.
Incorrect. Carbohydrates include large polysaccharides.
Incorrect. They occur naturally.

questions.question: Which two elements are present in carbohydrates in a fixed 2:1 ratio according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that H and O are present in a 2:1 ratio in carbohydrates, which gives the general formula (CH2O)n.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Nitrogen is not characteristic of carbohydrates.
Correct. H:O = 2:1.
Incorrect. Nitrogen is not characteristic of carbohydrates.
Incorrect. C:H ratio is not fixed at 2:1.
questions.hint: Which pair matches the water ratio?

questions.question: Ribose, a pentose found in nucleic acids, is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Ribose contains 5 carbons and an aldehyde group, so it is an aldopentose.
optionExplanations: Correct. Aldose + pentose.
Incorrect. Ribose is an aldose, not a ketose.
Incorrect. It has 5 carbons, not 6.
Incorrect. It has 5 carbons, not 4.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between D-erythrose and L-erythrose?
questions.explanation: D- and L-erythrose are non-superimposable mirror images of each other, making them enantiomers.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They have the same connectivity.
Correct. They are mirror images = enantiomers.
Incorrect. Epimers differ at only one chiral center; these differ at all chiral centers.
Incorrect. Anomers are α/β forms at the anomeric carbon.

questions.question: How many chiral carbons are present in a ketohexose such as fructose (in the open-chain form)?
questions.explanation: Fructose has 3 chiral carbons in the open-chain form (C3, C4, C5); C1 and C6 are CH2OH and C2 is the carbonyl, so none of those are chiral.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Only the terminal carbons and the C=O are achiral.
Incorrect. There are three chiral carbons.
Correct. C3, C4, C5 are chiral in open-chain fructose.
Incorrect. That would be the case for aldohexoses (glucose has 4).
questions.hint: Count between the CH2OH and C=O groups.

questions.question: If a compound has 3 chiral carbons, what is the maximum number of stereoisomers it can have?
questions.explanation: Using the formula 2^n with n = 3, the maximum is 2^3 = 8 stereoisomers.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. That is n, not 2^n.
Incorrect. Not a valid calculation here.
Correct. 2^3 = 8.
Incorrect. Not a valid calculation here.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about mutarotation is correct?
options: It is the interconversion of α- and β-anomers through the open-chain form in solution
It is the conversion of D-sugars into L-sugars
It is the hydrolysis of a glycosidic bond
It is the oxidation of the aldehyde group
questions.explanation: Mutarotation is the change in optical rotation observed when α- and β-anomers of a sugar interconvert in solution via the open-chain form until equilibrium is established.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the definition of mutarotation.
Incorrect. D/L interconversion does not occur spontaneously.
Incorrect. Hydrolysis of a glycosidic bond is a different reaction.
Incorrect. Oxidation is separate from mutarotation.

questions.question: The fact that α- and β-D-glucose interconvert in solution demonstrates that:
options: The open-chain form is accessible in solution
Glucose is not a reducing sugar
questions.explanation: Mutarotation occurs because the cyclic hemiacetal can open to the free aldehyde, allowing re-closure in either α or β form.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They can open via the free aldehyde.
Correct. The open-chain form is accessible.
Incorrect. C1 is the anomeric carbon.
Incorrect. Glucose is a reducing sugar.

questions.question: Which of the following monosaccharides would be classified as a ketose?
questions.explanation: Fructose contains a ketone group at C2 and is a ketose.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glucose is an aldose.
Incorrect. Galactose is an aldose.
Incorrect. Ribose is an aldose.
Correct. Fructose is a ketose.
questions.hint: Which one has a ketone group?

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about the structure of a monosaccharide ring in solution?
options: The ring contains one oxygen atom as part of the ring itself
The ring is always planar in 3D
questions.explanation: In the cyclic hemiacetal/hemiketal form, the ring oxygen comes from the hydroxyl group that attacked the carbonyl carbon.
optionExplanations: Correct. One oxygen is part of the ring.
Incorrect. The ring contains an oxygen.
Incorrect. Rings are puckered, not planar.
Incorrect. Oxygen is part of the ring.
questions.hint: The oxygen comes from an OH group.

questions.question: Which property of monosaccharides allows them to form syrups at high concentration?
options: Their many OH groups that strongly hydrogen bond with water
Their ability to form covalent bonds with water
questions.explanation: Glucose dissolves 1 g per 1 mL H2O to make a syrup, thanks to extensive hydrogen bonding between its OH groups and water.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Low MW alone does not explain syrup formation.
Correct. Extensive H-bonding with water.
Incorrect. Water does not form covalent bonds with sugars here.
Incorrect. Melting point is not the reason.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a reducing sugar?
